Somebody should research mechanical interlocks that prevent firmware change unless set to allow them.

Or just keep the industrial equipment on a separate network from the internet and air gap the two. At the end of the day someone can pull the data from the equipment network put it on a flash drive and post it to the rest of the network if you need multi site information. Nothing goes the other way except by approved and actually trained people. No one but the local guys care to check it more often anyhow no matter what they say about wanting to see it, well unless they are trying to micromanage a plant manager and those guys don't really care for that kind of behavior anyhow.

The problem with just air-gapping is that you have to allow people to be able to attach devices to retrieve the data. Sooner or later someone drops a USB drive in the parking lot and some operator thinks that will be handy to dump the data on to :) Better that they only have access to keyboard, mouse, and monitor and leave all maintenance to maintenance guys trained who know what they are doing and have a key to a cabinet around the computer. Of course that costs more money than just pushing updates down from the network but even with the enable/disable switch you still have the option to leave it enabled if you don't think the extra cost is justified to have to visit each machine in person to update.

To be honest I think a real interlock that requires whatever moves to be physically locked to do an update and power back up would be even better. Some asshole will write firmware sooner or later that is designed to injure the person loading it.

The thing is that there becomes two choices to maintenance then they can go flip switches all over for each update or just leave them flipped and update anytime, one takes less work. If you lock out use when in update mode Someone will flip that switch before a holiday break and then it just doesn't work when they come back holding up production.

Yes data has to go to the machine at some point to update it, but that can be locked down to two computers (one on a shelf in IT as a backup). The other you are going to have to train and pick someone that knows what they are doing instead of having the HR secretary do it. Air gaps suck as they are annoying to work around but they are effective when done right and the network is secured from randomly plugged in systems.

I suppose if you could cut the receive pair or use some other method to push the data out only to somewhere else and collect it from that point and that would be OK. Randomly plugged in anything presents a risk including storage. The centrifuges in Iran were probably air-gapped and some idiot probably plugged something in like a usb stick they found in the parking lot.

Imperfect but simply having no extra active ports on the network and all existing ports require a specific MAC, then all but the one device would have CD/DVD/USB disabled, and that one would have a person that understands technology (not IT specifically but understands the risks or unknown devices, and understand that they are the first place people will be looking if something gets in). I know MAC spoofing is still a risk but we limit it down to someone having to be in the building and have the knowledge to get the MAC and spoof it, just the physical access needed cuts it down on attack vectors since there would be no internet pages that are infected or emails since those can't get to.
